kurals.tamil:
மாலையோ அல்லை மணந்தார் உயிருண்ணும்
வேலைநீ வாழி பொழுது.
kurals.transliteration:
Maalaiyo allai manandhaar uyirunnum
vaelainee vaazhi pozhudhu.
kurals.meaning: O evening hour, long may you live! You are no gentle evening at all, but a killing time that devours the lives of wives whose husbands are away.
kurals.elementary: Think of the time of day you used to love most, like when a parent came home and played with you. If that parent had to go far away for a long time, the same hour might suddenly feel sad and heavy instead of happy. The wife in this verse feels that way about evening.
kurals.university: Chapter 123, poḻutu kaṇṭu iraṅkal (‘lamenting on seeing the hour’), belongs to the kaṟpiyal (wedded love) section: the wife, separated from her husband, finds that dusk (mālai), once the hour of reunion, now sharpens her grief. The opening couplet is an ironic apostrophe: vāḻi (‘may you live long!’) is a blessing turned to reproach, and maṇantār (‘those who were united/wedded’) is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as women who knew union and now live apart. The key word vēlai is read two ways: Varadarasanar and Kesikan take it as ‘time, end-time’ (muṭivu kālam), while Mu. Karunanidhi reads vēl, ‘spear’, which is also Pope’s choice (‘a spear that doth devour / The souls of brides’). The couplet text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (the latter spells the chapter title as two words, poḻutukaṇṭu iraṅkal).

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the lake Pampa in springtime, Rama, separated from Sita, finds that the blossoming trees, the bird-calls and the fragrant breeze, which should delight him, only inflame his grief, and he tells Lakshmana that the season itself is tormenting him.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki shows a lover for whom the loveliest scenes of nature become instruments of pain because the beloved is absent.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s evening, Rama’s springtime is a beautiful hour that has turned into an assailant of the separated heart.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; strong match on a delightful time turned painful by separation, though it is spring rather than evening and the sufferer is the husband.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs, read in Christian tradition as an image of love between Christ and the soul, gives the bride’s ache when night comes and the beloved is absent.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife suffers in exactly that hour when she reaches for her husband and finds him gone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; strong match on night-time longing for an absent beloved, though the verse does not personify the hour as a killer.

islam.quote_or_event: “And from the evil of darkness when it settles”
islam.explanation: In Surat al-Falaq the believer seeks refuge in God from the harm that comes as darkness falls.
islam.tie_back: The Kural also treats the coming of dusk as a menace that preys on the vulnerable, though Islam answers it with refuge in God rather than lament.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the shared idea is nightfall as a dangerous hour, but the verse has nothing to do with lovers’ separation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “She weepeth sore in the night, And her tears are on her cheeks; She hath none to comfort her Among all her lovers”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations pictures Jerusalem as a forsaken woman whose grief is sharpest at night, when no one comforts her.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife is likewise a woman whose sorrow peaks as darkness comes and her beloved is not there.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; close match on a woman weeping at night for lack of her beloved, though the woman is a figure for the city.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names separation from what is dear as a direct cause of pain and advises loosening the bond.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows that pain at its sharpest; Buddhism diagnoses its root in attachment, so the fit is real but the response differs.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; matches the suffering of separation, but the Dhammapada prescribes non-attachment where the Kural simply laments.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira’s teaching warns that pleasures which are sweet at first turn deadly in the end.
jainism.tie_back: The evening that once brought the wife sweetness now ‘devours lives’, which is the very reversal the Kimpaka simile describes.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; good structural parallel (sweet turned lethal), though the Jain verse condemns pleasure rather than mourning a lost one.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope tells the disguised Odysseus that by day she can distract herself with her work and household, but when night comes and everyone sleeps she lies awake and sharp cares crowd her grieving heart.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s faithful wife finds that the coming of night, not the day, is when the absence of her husband becomes unbearable.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s complaint exactly: the day is endurable, but the closing hour turns on the waiting wife.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 19.509-517 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; very close match on a separated wife whose grief is worst at nightfall.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes tells how the original double humans were cut in two, and each half so longed for its other that the halves clung together and began to die of hunger and idleness, unwilling to do anything apart.
philosophy.explanation: The myth makes the longing of separated lovers literally life-threatening.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s claim that the evening ‘eats the lives’ of separated wives speaks the same idea of love-longing as something that can consume life itself.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 191a-b (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; good fit on longing as deadly, but it is a comic myth about origins, not a lament at dusk.

kurals.tamil:
புன்கண்ணை வாழி மருள்மாலை எம்கேள்போல்
வன்கண்ண தோநின் துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Punkannai vaazhi marulmaalai emkaelpoal
vankanna dhoanin thunai.
kurals.meaning: Bless you, bewildered dusk, your eyes look as dim and sad as mine; is your partner as hard-hearted as my husband?
kurals.elementary: Sometimes when we are sad, the whole world seems sad with us: a grey sky looks like it is crying too. The wife looks at the fading evening light and asks it, kindly, ‘Did someone leave you too?’
kurals.university: Here the wife turns from accusing the evening to commiserating with it: mālai is marul (‘bewildered, dim’, the twilight in which day and night mingle, as Solomon Pappaiah explains) and puṉkaṇṇai (‘you have afflicted, dull eyes’), a picture of fading light as tear-dimmed sight. Kēḷ means a kinsman or intimate, here the husband, and vaṉkaṇṇatu (‘hard-eyed, pitiless’) mirrors puṉkaṇ: her eyes are sad because his are hard. Varadarasanar and Kesikan read the question as ‘is your companion too as merciless as my lover?’, while Pappaiah explicitly asks whether the evening’s husband is cruel like hers. Pope: ‘Thine eye is sad; Hail, doubtful hour of eventide! / Of cruel eye, as is my spouse, is too thy bride?’ The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the close of the Meghaduta, the exiled Yaksha, who has spoken to a passing cloud as a friend and asked it to carry his message to his wife, blesses the cloud that it may never be parted, even for a moment, from its own beloved, the lightning.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s separated lover treats a piece of the sky as a fellow being with a spouse of its own.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife does the same with the evening, imagining that it too has a partner and may share her suffering.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous classical poem; close parallel of a separated lover addressing nature as one with its own mate, though the Yaksha blesses the cloud rather than pitying it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Paul asks believers to share one another’s joys and sorrows.
christianity.tie_back: The wife imagines the dusk ‘weeping with her’, the fellow-feeling Paul commends, though here it is projected onto nature.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; only a partial fit on shared sorrow, with nothing about lovers or the evening.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes Jacob’s eyes clouded by long grief for his absent son.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s dim-eyed dusk (puṉkaṇ) is the same image: eyes dulled by sorrow for someone far away.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; strong match on eyes dimmed by separation-grief, though the bond is parent and child.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For these things I weep; Mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water; Because the comforter is far from me”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations voices grief through the eye, flowing with tears because the one who should comfort is far away.
judaism.tie_back: The wife sees in the evening’s ‘sad eye’ her own tear-dimmed eye, both caused by a comforter who has gone far off.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; good match on weeping eyes and a distant comforter, though the speaker is the personified city.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that not seeing the one we love is itself a form of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife and the evening she pities are both caught in that pain of not seeing the beloved.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; matches the pain of absence, but does not touch the Kural’s device of pitying nature as a fellow sufferer.

jainism.quote_or_event: Prince Arishtanemi (Neminatha), riding to his wedding with Rajimati, hears the cries of animals penned for the wedding feast, has them released and renounces the world; Rajimati is left grieving her bridegroom before she too takes the vows.
jainism.explanation: The Jain canon tells of a bride whose betrothed left her for a higher calling, a departure that seemed hard to her though it was born of compassion.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati could have asked the Kural’s question, ‘is your partner as hard-hearted as mine?’, though Jain tradition frames Neminatha’s leaving as the opposite of cruelty.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested Jain narrative, not checked against the text in this session; the abandoned-bride situation fits, but Jainism praises the departure the Kural’s wife resents.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Spurned by Narcissus, the nymph Echo hides in lonely caves and wastes away with sleepless grief until her body is gone and only her voice remains among the hills.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid turns a rejected lover’s sorrow into a feature of the landscape itself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife sees a fellow sufferer in the dimming evening, much as Greek myth sees one in the lonely echo.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best match: Echo personifies love-grief in nature, but she is rejected rather than separated, and no one asks her about her partner.

philosophy.quote_or_event: John Ruskin coined the term ‘pathetic fallacy’ for the way strong emotion leads a poet to credit nature with human feelings, as when a grieving speaker sees cruelty or sorrow in the sea, the crocus or the sky.
philosophy.explanation: Ruskin analyses the habit of the passionate mind to lend its own mood to the outside world.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s question to the ‘sad-eyed’ dusk is a textbook case of the pathetic fallacy, used deliberately by the poet to show how grief colours perception.
philosophy.source: John Ruskin, Modern Painters, vol. 3, part 4, ch. 12 ‘Of the Pathetic Fallacy’ (1856) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known essay; it names precisely the device this couplet uses, though Ruskin is often critical of it.

kurals.tamil:
பனிஅரும்பிப் பைதல்கொள் மாலை துனிஅரும்பித்
துன்பம் வளர வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Paniarumpip paidhalkol maalai thuniarumpith
thunpam valara varum.
kurals.meaning: The pale evening, beaded with dew, now arrives so that weariness of life sprouts in me and my sorrow keeps on growing.
kurals.elementary: Picture tiny dewdrops forming on leaves as the sun goes down. The wife says her sadness grows the same way, drop by drop, every evening, until it feels much bigger than it did in the morning.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a parallel of two ‘buddings’: paṉi arumpi (dew forms like buds) and tuṉi arumpi (aversion or distress begins to sprout), so that the evening’s dew and the wife’s grief swell together. Paital koḷ describes the evening taking on a sallow, faded hue, recalling the wife’s own pasalai (love-pallor) of chapter 119. Commentators divide on time: Varadarasanar and Kesikan read the whole as the present evening, while Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi contrast an earlier evening that came ‘trembling and pale’ while the husband was near with the present one that brings mounting sorrow; Pope’s couplet explanation follows the latter (‘once came in with trembling and dimness’). Pope: ‘With buds of chilly dew wan evening’s shade enclose; / My anguish buds space and all my sorrow grows.’ Both web texts agree on the wording.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda, Radha’s friend tells Krishna that in his absence the cool things of evening, sandal paste, moonlight and the soft breeze, feel to Radha like fire and poison, and her suffering grows night by night.
hinduism.explanation: The great Sanskrit poem of viraha (love in separation) makes the soothing features of dusk into torments for the waiting beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s dewy evening, which should cool, instead makes the wife’s sorrow grow, exactly the reversal Jayadeva paints for Radha.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known viraha motif in the poem; strong thematic match, though I have not checked the exact canto wording in this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day.”
christianity.explanation: Job, in his suffering, dreads the coming of night because it stretches his misery until dawn (the KJV margin notes the Hebrew as ‘the evening be measured’).
christianity.tie_back: Like Job, the Kural’s wife finds that the evening does not bring rest but lengthens and deepens her distress.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; good fit on night-time suffering growing, though Job’s grief is not about a beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob, still separated from Joseph, voices a grief that has kept growing, and turns it toward God.
islam.tie_back: The wife’s sorrow likewise keeps ‘growing’; Islam’s model is to pour that mounting grief out before God rather than before the evening.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; matches prolonged grief of separation, but has no evening imagery and the relationship is parental.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I am weary with my groaning; Every night make I my bed to swim; I melt away my couch with my tears.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist describes sorrow that returns and swells each night.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife also finds that each nightfall brings a fresh and larger flood of grief.
judaism.source: Psalms 6:7 (JPS 1917, via Sefaria; 6:6 in KJV numbering)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; good match on nightly, growing grief, though the Psalm’s cause is illness and enemies rather than a lover.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to the affection from which it grows.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural shows grief ‘budding’ and growing each evening; the Dhammapada names the root it grows from.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; matches the growth of grief from love, but offers a cure the Kural does not seek.

jainism.quote_or_event: “In the same way he who hates ‘colours,’ incurs a long succession of pains; when his mind is filled with hatred, he accumulates Karman which in the end again produces misery.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that aversion to what we perceive is as binding as desire and lengthens our suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The wife now loathes the very sight of evening, and Jain teaching would say that this aversion is itself what makes her sorrow keep growing.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a doctrinal reading of the growing distress rather than a direct parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After her son Memnon is killed at Troy, Aurora (Eos), goddess of the dawn, never stops mourning him, and Ovid says her tears still fall over the whole world as the morning dew.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth explains dew as a goddess’s tears of grief for one she has lost.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘dew budding’ at dusk, rising alongside the wife’s sorrow, links dew and grief in the same way.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; striking match on dew as grief, though it is morning dew and a mother’s grief.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines longing (desiderium) as the desire to possess a thing that is fed by remembering it and, at the same time, checked by remembering other things that exclude its presence.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, longing is a painful tension between memory of the beloved and awareness that the beloved is absent.
philosophy.tie_back: Each evening reminds the wife both of her husband and of his absence, so by Spinoza’s account her longing must grow, as the Kural says.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Definitions of the Affects 32 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.H.M. Elwes)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a definition; precise account of the mechanism of longing, though abstract rather than poetic.

kurals.tamil:
காதலர் இல்வழி மாலை கொலைக்களத்து
ஏதிலர் போல வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaadhalar ilvazhi maalai kolaikkalaththu
aedhilar poala varum.
kurals.meaning: When my beloved is not here, the evening comes at me like enemies advancing on a killing ground.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a game where a scary character slowly walks toward you and you cannot run. When the wife is alone, the evening feels like that: it creeps closer and closer, and she dreads it.
kurals.university: The simile is military and stark: kolaikkaḷam is a ‘field of slaughter’ or execution ground, and ētilar are strangers or foes, so evening approaches the lonely wife like men coming to kill. Kesikan glosses ētilar as highway robbers (āṟalaippār) at a place of murder, Varadarasanar as enemies, and Karunanidhi shifts the image to an enemy’s raised sword; Solomon Pappaiah adds the contrast implicit in the chapter, that the same evening once made her life flourish when her husband was home. Pope’s couplet runs: ‘When absent is my love, the evening hour descends, / As when an alien host to field of battle wends.’ Both web sources give ētilar; a song setting by P. A. Muthukrishnan quoted on thirukkural.net sings it as ētilār, a lyrical lengthening rather than a textual variant.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ashoka grove of Lanka, Sita, separated from Rama, is surrounded by fierce rakshasi guards who threaten to kill and devour her if she will not yield to Ravana, and in her despair she longs for death.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki places the separated wife literally among would-be killers, her grief for Rama sharpened by their menace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife only feels the evening as such killers; Sita lives the image, alone and threatened while her husband is far away.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, the rakshasis’ threats to Sita (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; vivid parallel of a separated wife beset by killers, though the threat is real rather than an evening simile.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prepare ye war against her; arise, and let us go up at noon. Woe unto us! for the day goeth away, for the shadows of the evening are stretched out.”
christianity.explanation: In Jeremiah, invaders preparing to attack cry out as the evening shadows lengthen, linking the fall of evening with the onset of assault.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s evening also arrives with the lengthening shadows of an attacking enemy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the pairing of evening shadows and enemy attack fits the image, but the context is a siege, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: “When night falls (or it is evening), keep your children close to you for the devils spread out at that time.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet treats nightfall as a dangerous hour when harmful forces spread abroad.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise feels the coming of evening as the arrival of hostile powers.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; shares the image of evening as a time when harm advances, but concerns children and devils, not a lonely wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not be afraid of the terror by night, Nor of the arrow that flieth by day; Of the pestilence that walketh in darkness, Nor of the destruction that wasteth at noonday.”
judaism.explanation: Psalm 91 names the terror that walks in the dark and promises that one sheltered by God need not fear it.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife experiences just such a ‘terror by night’ approaching her; the Psalm answers it with trust in divine protection.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; matches night as an advancing destroyer, but the Psalm is about protection, not longing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada compares death to a great flood that sweeps away a sleeping village, carrying off the person whose mind clings to children and cattle.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism pictures death advancing suddenly on those absorbed in their attachments.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s evening comes like killers to a heart wholly bound up in an absent love, the clinging mind the Dhammapada warns about.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked against the text in this session; the deadly approach fits, but the verse is about death and attachment in general.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The mind of those who always live in unfrequented lodgings, who eat low food, and who subdue their senses, will not be attacked by the foe, Love, who is vanquished as disease is by medicine.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana calls Love a foe that attacks the undisciplined mind.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels herself attacked at evening as if by enemies; Jain teaching names the real attacker as love itself.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; shares the image of love as an attacking enemy, though the Jain verse addresses monks, not a wife.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Hesiod’s Theogony, Night (Nyx) gives birth to hateful Doom, black Fate and Death, and to Sleep and the tribe of Dreams.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth makes Night the mother of the powers that destroy human life.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s evening, coming like killers, is the same dark power that Hesiod sees as the mother of Death.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Theogony 211-212 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known genealogy; matches night as deadly, but has no connection to love or separation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius says that as children tremble and fear everything in the blind darkness, so we adults in daylight sometimes fear things no more real than what children dread in the dark.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet treats dread of the dark as a product of the mind, to be dispelled by understanding.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife dreads the evening as if it were an assassin; Lucretius would say the terror comes from within, not from the hour.
philosophy.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 2.55-58 (paraphrase; cf. tr. W.H.D. Rouse)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; fits the fear of darkness, but treats it as irrational rather than as love’s grief.

kurals.tamil:
காலைக்குச் செய்தநன்று என்கொல் எவன்கொல்யான்
மாலைக்குச் செய்த பகை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaalaikkuch cheydhanandru enkol evankolyaan
maalaikkuch cheydha pakai.
kurals.meaning: What kindness did I ever do the morning, that it treats me gently, and what wrong did I do the evening, that it torments me so?
kurals.elementary: Have you ever felt that one part of the day is friendly and another part is mean to you? The wife feels mornings are kind and evenings are cruel, and she asks, puzzled, what she did to deserve it.
kurals.university: The couplet is a pair of rhetorical questions built on the parallel kālaikku / mālaikku (‘to the morning / to the evening’) and naṉṟu / pakai (‘a good turn / enmity’): the wife treats the two times of day as persons who repay her for imagined past conduct. Varadarasanar glosses pakai as ‘a hostile evil’ done to the evening, and Kalaignar adds the implied reason: love-pain grows sharpest when evening comes. The playful logic of reciprocity echoes the Kural’s ethical chapters on returning good for good, now applied absurdly to the hours. Pope: ‘O morn, how have I won thy grace? thou bring’st relief / O eve, why art thou foe! thou dost renew my grief.’ The text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that pleasure and pain come and go with the turning of times and must be borne with equanimity.
hinduism.tie_back: The wife feels the morning as friend and the evening as foe; the Gita answers that such alternations arise from perception and pass in their season.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; good fit on pain and pleasure tied to changing times, but the Gita counsels endurance where the Kural laments.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is of the LORD’S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.”
christianity.explanation: In the midst of lament, the poet finds that mercy returns fresh with each morning.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise feels the morning as a kindly presence set against a cruel evening.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; matches the morning as a time of relief, but the evening-as-enemy half has no counterpart.

islam.quote_or_event: “By the morning brightness, And [by] the night when it covers with darkness, Your Lord has not taken leave of you, [O Muhammad], nor has He detested [you].”
islam.explanation: Revealed when the Prophet feared he had been abandoned, Surat ad-Duha sets morning against night and reassures him he has not been forsaken.
islam.tie_back: The wife sets morning against evening and feels herself abandoned; the Qur’an uses the same pair of times to deny abandonment.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; strong parallel of morning and night framed around fear of being left, though the one absent is God, not a husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For His anger is but for a moment, His favour is for a life-time; weeping may tarry for the night, but joy cometh in the morning.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist sets the weeping of the night against the joy of the morning.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s very contrast: night brings tears and the morning brings relief.
judaism.source: Psalms 30:6 (JPS 1917, via Sefaria; 30:5 in KJV numbering)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; close match on night as the time of weeping and morning as relief, though the cause is divine anger, not separation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The opening verses of the Dhammapada teach that the mind goes before all mental states: if one acts or speaks with a corrupted mind, suffering follows as the wheel follows the ox’s foot, and with a pure mind, happiness follows like a shadow.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhism locates the source of pain and joy in the mind, not in outside conditions.
buddhism.tie_back: The wife asks what she did to the evening; the Dhammapada would answer that the hour is neutral and the suffering is shaped within.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of famous verses; a doctrinal answer to the Kural’s question rather than a parallel to its feeling.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who passionately hates (a colour), will at the same moment suffer pain. It is the fault of an undisciplined man that he is annoyed (by a colour); it is not the ‘colour’ itself that annoys him.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that the objects of the senses do not themselves cause pain; our passion toward them does.
jainism.tie_back: The wife asks what she did to make the evening her enemy; Jain teaching answers that the evening has done nothing, the pain lies in the mind’s attachment and aversion.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a direct answer to the Kural’s question about why a neutral hour seems hostile.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus is favoured throughout his wanderings by Athena yet pursued by the unrelenting anger of Poseidon, so that one god helps and another harms him, and he endures years of suffering for a grudge he only half understands.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s hero lives between a friendly power and a hostile one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels the same split, with a kindly morning and a hostile evening, and asks what she has done to earn each.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 1.19-21, 1.68-79 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known framing; matches the friend-and-foe structure, but Poseidon’s anger has a known cause and nothing to do with love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus teaches that people are disturbed not by things themselves but by their judgements about things, so that one should blame neither others nor circumstances for one’s distress.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic locates the source of suffering in our opinions rather than in events.
philosophy.tie_back: The evening is not truly the wife’s enemy; on Epictetus’s view it is her judgement of the evening, coloured by absence, that wounds her.
philosophy.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. George Long)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous maxim; a clear philosophical answer to the Kural’s question, though it reframes rather than shares her grief.

kurals.tamil:
மாலைநோய் செய்தல் மணந்தார் அகலாத
காலை அறிந்த திலேன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Maalainoi seydhal manandhaar akalaadha
kaalai arindha thilaen.
kurals.meaning: While my husband had not yet left my side, I never knew that evening could bring such suffering.
kurals.elementary: When your best friend is next to you, you do not notice how quiet the house is. Only when they go away do you notice the silence. The wife says she never knew evenings could hurt until her husband left.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on the contrast between maṇantār akalāta kālai (‘the time when he who wed me had not departed’) and the present, in which mālai nōy, ‘the evening sickness’, has made itself known. Kālai here is a pun: in the previous couplet it meant ‘morning’, but here it is the old Tamil word for ‘time, season’, a play the commentators make explicit by glossing it as kālam. Solomon Pappaiah stresses that the same evening once gave her joy; Varadarasanar and Kesikan read aṟintatilēṉ as ‘I did not know at all’. Pope: ‘The pangs that evening brings I never knew, / Till he, my wedded spouse, from me withdrew.’ Both web sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Nala, ruined at dice, slips away at night while Damayanti sleeps in the forest; she wakes alone, searches for him, and laments that she never imagined he would leave her.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata’s tale shows a devoted wife who discovers the full pain of the night only after her husband has gone.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Damayanti, the Kural’s wife learned what night-time grief was only after her husband left her side.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; good match on discovering grief after a husband’s departure, though Nala’s leaving is an abandonment, not a journey for wealth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus explains that there is no mourning while the bridegroom is present, but sorrow will come when he is taken away.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural states the same truth from the wife’s side: while her bridegroom was with her she knew no evening sorrow, and it came only when he left.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; close match on no grief while the bridegroom is present and grief once he is gone, though Jesus speaks of himself figuratively.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the heart of Moses’ mother became empty [of all else]. She was about to disclose [the matter concerning] him had We not bound fast her heart that she would be of the believers.”
islam.explanation: After setting her infant afloat, Moses’ mother feels the full emptiness of separation, and God steadies her heart.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise discovers an emptiness she had never known once her beloved is gone.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a real parallel of the heart emptied by separation, but the bond is mother and child and there is no evening motif.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song of Songs discovers his absence only after the moment of nearness has passed.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife also learns the depth of her love’s pain only when he has gone and she cannot find him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; good match on a woman’s grief on finding her beloved gone, though without the idea that she had never known such pain before.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In Ashvaghosha’s Buddhacarita, when the charioteer Chandaka returns without Prince Siddhartha, his wife Yashodhara falls to the ground and laments bitterly that her husband has gone and left her alone.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist epic gives voice to the wife whose life changed in an instant when her husband departed.
buddhism.tie_back: Yashodhara, like the Kural’s wife, learns the full weight of grief only when her husband has gone away.
buddhism.source: Ashvaghosha, Buddhacarita, canto 8 (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell, SBE 49)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against the text in this session; strong situational match, though Siddhartha leaves for liberation, not wealth.

jainism.quote_or_event: “How can a man who passionately desires ‘colours,’ be happy while he gets, keeps, uses, loses, and misses (those things). Even when he enjoys them, he is never satisfied.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that whatever we cling to will bring pain at the stages of losing and missing it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife has reached the ‘losing and missing’ stage, and finds a pain she never suspected while she still possessed his company.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches pain discovered in losing and missing, though framed as a warning against attachment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Laodamia, newly married to Protesilaus, writes to him after he sails for Troy, describing how his departure has turned her days and nights into anxious grief she never knew while he was home.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s heroine is a young wife who learns the meaning of separation only when her husband goes away.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife and Laodamia make the same discovery: the pain of absence was unknown until the husband left.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known poem; close situational match, though I have not verified specific lines in this session.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy reminds Boethius that in every adversity of fortune, the most wretched kind of misfortune is to have once been happy.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius observes that past happiness sharpens present loss.
philosophy.tie_back: The wife’s evenings hurt because they were once happy with her husband, exactly the bitterness Boethius describes.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2, prose 4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.R. James)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous line; strong match on former joy deepening present grief.

kurals.tamil:
காலை அரும்பிப் பகலெல்லாம் போதாகி
மாலை மலரும்இந் நோய்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaalai arumpip pakalellaam poadhaaki
maalai malarumin noai.
kurals.meaning: This love-sickness buds in the morning, swells all day into a full bud, and bursts into bloom at evening.
kurals.elementary: Watch a flower: first a tiny bud, then a bigger bud, then it opens wide. The wife says her missing-him feeling grows the same way each day: small in the morning, bigger at noon, and wide open by evening.
kurals.university: One of the most admired images in the Kāmattuppāl, the couplet maps the growth of nōy (the love-sickness) onto the three stages of a flower: arumpu (bud) in the morning, pōtu (the full bud on the point of opening; Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss it as pērarumpu, ‘large bud’) through the day, and malar (open bloom) at evening. The irony is pointed: the flower, symbol of love’s beauty, becomes the shape of love’s pain, and its daily cycle explains why the evening is worst. Solomon Pappaiah calls the disease ‘this flower of love-suffering’, and Karunanidhi generalises it to love itself. Pope: ‘My grief at morn a bud, all day an opening flower, / Full-blown expands in evening hour.’ The text is identical on both web sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When You go off to the forest during the day, a tiny fraction of a second becomes like a millennium for us because we cannot see You.”
hinduism.explanation: In their song of separation, the gopis tell Krishna that every moment of the day without him swells into an age.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s love-sickness that grows through the day toward evening, the gopis’ longing expands hour by hour while Krishna is away.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.31.15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami, via vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; good match on longing swelling through the day of absence, though without the flower image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride in the Song of Songs names her longing as a sickness.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural too calls love-longing a nōy, a disease, and traces its growth through the day.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; matches love-longing as sickness, but lacks the image of its daily growth.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sons warn that his unending remembrance of his lost son will grow into a fatal illness.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise describes longing for an absent loved one as a sickness that keeps growing.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; matches longing as a growing sickness, though the bond is parental.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick; But desire fulfilled is a tree of life.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that longing which is put off becomes a sickness of the heart, while its fulfilment is like a living, flowering tree.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife suffers the first half of the proverb, and pictures her deferred longing as a plant that buds and blooms into sickness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; good match on deferred longing as heart-sickness, with a plant image in the second half.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the sorrow that comes from craving to vegetation springing up after rain.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural also pictures love-sorrow as a growing plant, though as a flower that opens by evening.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; striking parallel of sorrow growing like a plant, though the Dhammapada condemns the craving behind it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When he is not satisfied with those ‘colours,’ and his craving for them grows stronger and stronger, he will become discontented, and unhappy by dint of his discontent”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana describes how craving, once unsatisfied, grows stronger and brings ever-deeper unhappiness.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness grows from bud to bloom in exactly this way, stronger and stronger through the day.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (quoted in part); good match on unsatisfied longing growing steadily, without the flower image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros the limb-loosener who shakes her, a bittersweet creature against which there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek lyric presents love as a force that overpowers the body, both sweet and painful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness, which blooms into full pain by evening, is the same bittersweet power Sappho names.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous fragment; matches love as an overpowering sickness, but not its daily growth or separation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates describes how the soul in love begins to grow its feathers again: the growth throbs and aches like teething, and when the beloved is absent the sprouting points are pinched shut and the soul is stung with pain.
philosophy.explanation: Plato pictures love as an organic growth within the soul, painful when the beloved is away.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s love-sickness also grows like a living thing, budding and opening, and hurts most in absence.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 251b-e (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; strong match on love as a painful growth intensified by absence.

kurals.tamil:
அழல்போலும் மாலைக்குத் தூதாகி ஆயன்
குழல்போலும் கொல்லும் படை.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhalpoalum maalaikkuth thoodhaaki aayan
kuzhalpoalum kollum padai.
kurals.meaning: Even the herdsman’s flute, acting as the herald of this fire-like evening, has become a weapon that kills me.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a song you used to love can make you sad if it reminds you of someone who is far away. The herdsman plays his flute every evening; it used to sound sweet to the wife, but now it tells her that the lonely evening is coming, so it hurts to hear.
kurals.university: At dusk the herdsman (āyaṉ) plays his flute (kuḻal) as he brings the cattle home, and in classical Tamil poetics this belongs to the mullai landscape, whose mood is patient waiting (iruttal) and whose hour is evening. The flute becomes the tūtu (herald, envoy) of a mālai that burns like aḻal (fire), and so a paṭai (weapon) that kills; the repeated pōlum is read by the commentators as a particle of emphasis (‘the flute too’), not as ‘like’. Solomon Pappaiah notes that the flute once sounded sweet, and Karunanidhi likens its notes to the clang of a weapon. Pope: ‘The shepherd’s pipe is like a murderous weapon, to my ear, / For it proclaims the hour of ev’ning’s fiery anguish near.’ Both web sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Venu-gita, the gopis of Vraja, hearing the flute that the cowherd Krishna plays as he wanders with the cows, are so overwhelmed by longing that they can only describe to one another, in agitation, the power of its music.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata makes the cowherd’s flute the very sound of love’s longing for those separated from him.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s āyaṉ kuḻal is exactly a cowherd’s flute; for the gopis as for the wife, its music stirs unbearable longing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter; very close image (a herdsman’s flute rousing longing), though for the gopis it is also a joy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep.”
christianity.explanation: Job laments that the instruments which once gave him joy now sound only grief.
christianity.tie_back: The herdsman’s flute, once sweet to the Kural’s wife, has likewise turned into a voice of mourning, even a weapon.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; close match on music turned to grief, though Job’s sorrow is not about a lover.

islam.quote_or_event: “HEARKEN to the reed-flute, how it complains, Lamenting its banishment from its home: ‘Ever since they tore me from my osier bed, My plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears.’”
islam.explanation: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed flute whose music is a lament of separation, read in Sufi tradition as the soul’s longing for God.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s flute and Rumi’s reed both sing of separation and wound those who hear it.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book 1, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield, 1898)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong match on the flute as the voice of separation, though Rumi’s longing is mystical and the flute laments rather than kills.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Upon the willows in the midst thereof We hanged up our harps. For there they that led us captive asked of us words of song, And our tormentors asked of us mirth: ‘Sing us one of the songs of Zion.’ How shall we sing the LORD’S song In a foreign land?”
judaism.explanation: The exiles by the rivers of Babylon find that music, once joyful, has become unbearable in separation from home.
judaism.tie_back: For the separated wife too, music that once delighted now only deepens her pain.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; good match on music made painful by separation, though the separation is from Zion, not a spouse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha’s half-brother Nanda, ordained as a monk, grows discontented and wants to return to lay life because he keeps remembering the parting words of his beautiful Sakyan bride, who asked him to hurry back.
buddhism.explanation: The Udana shows how a single remembered sound of the beloved can keep longing alive and painful.
buddhism.tie_back: The flute’s notes act on the Kural’s wife as the bride’s parting words act on Nanda, reviving longing each time they are recalled.
buddhism.source: Udana 3.2 (Nanda Sutta) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Next-best match, paraphrased; shares a sensory reminder rekindling longing, but there is no flute and the Buddha cures Nanda of it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As an impassioned deer allured (by a song) rushes into death, without being satisfied with the sound.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana compares one enslaved by the sense of hearing to a deer drawn to its death by music.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife finds the herdsman’s music literally a ‘killing weapon’; the Jain verse uses the same image of a song that leads to death.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; given in Jacobi’s summary note to verses 35-47)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; striking parallel of music as deadly, though the Jain verse blames the listener’s passion rather than the music.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Syrinx flees the god Pan and is turned into marsh reeds; as Pan sighs over them, the wind in the reeds makes a soft, mournful sound, and he binds reeds of different lengths into the pipe that bears her name.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells how the shepherd’s pipe was born from a love that ended in loss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The herdsman’s pipe in the Kural also carries the sound of love’s loss, which is why it wounds the waiting wife.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth; good match on the shepherd’s pipe as a sound of lost love, though Pan is the pursuer, not a waiting spouse.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates proposes to banish the dirge-like musical modes, such as the Mixolydian, because music of lament makes the listener’s soul sorrowful and soft.
philosophy.explanation: Plato holds that musical modes have direct power over the emotions of those who hear them.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural shows that power at its extreme: the flute’s evening music can wound the grieving wife like a weapon.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic 398d-399a (paraphrase; cf. tr. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; matches music’s emotional power, but Plato is legislating, not describing love-grief.

kurals.tamil:
பதிமருண்டு பைதல் உழக்கும் மதிமருண்டு
மாலை படர்தரும் போழ்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Padhimarundu paidhal uzhakkum madhimarundu
maalai padardharum poazhdhu.
kurals.meaning: When evening spreads over everything and clouds the mind, it seems that the whole town, bewildered, suffers in sorrow just as I do.
kurals.elementary: When you are very sad, it can feel as if the whole world is sad with you, even the street and the houses. As evening darkness spreads over the town, the wife feels that everyone there must be as unhappy as she is.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two phrases with maruṇṭu (‘bewildered, confused’): pati maruṇṭu, ‘the town bewildered’, and mati maruṇṭu, ‘the mind bewildered’, as evening ‘spreads’ (paṭartarum) over all. Varadarasanar, Kesikan and Karunanidhi take mati as ‘understanding’, so that the dusk confuses the mind and the whole town seems to share the wife’s grief; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a prediction that from now on the whole town will suffer as she has. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone takes mati as ‘moon’ (the moon itself bewildered), an alternative reading worth noting. Pope: ‘If evening’s shades, that darken all my soul, extend; / From this afflicted town will would of grief ascend.’ The text is identical on both web sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Rama leaves Ayodhya for exile, the whole city falls into mourning: the citizens weep, households neglect their fires and food, and Ayodhya seems lifeless in its grief for him.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki shows one departure plunging an entire city into shared sorrow.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife imagines the whole town grieving with her at dusk; Ayodhya actually does so at Rama’s parting.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda, the city’s grief at Rama’s exile (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; strong match on a whole town sharing grief over an absence, though the grief is real rather than imagined.

christianity.quote_or_event: “In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.”
christianity.explanation: Matthew uses Jeremiah’s image of a whole town filled with a woman’s inconsolable lament.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s wife likewise feels her grief spreading until the whole town seems to share it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; shares a woman’s grief filling a town, but the cause is the death of children.

islam.quote_or_event: “You see the believers as regards their being merciful among themselves and showing love among themselves and being kind, resembling one body, so that, if any part of the body is not well then the whole body shares the sleeplessness (insomnia) and fever with it.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes a community bound so closely that one member’s pain is felt by all.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s wife imagines exactly this: her evening sleeplessness and sorrow spreading to the whole town.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; good match on one person’s suffering shared by all, though the hadith describes an ideal of compassion, not a lover’s projection.

judaism.quote_or_event: “How doth the city sit solitary, That was full of people! How is she become as a widow!”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations opens by picturing the whole city as a woman bereft of her husband.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural blends the woman and the town in the same way: as dusk falls, the whole town seems to share her bereaved grief.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; close parallel of a city and a forsaken woman merging in grief, though it mourns a national catastrophe.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Kisa Gotami, mad with grief for her dead child, is told by the Buddha to bring a mustard seed from a house where no one has died; going from door to door through the whole town, she finds that every household has known loss, and her grief is transformed.
buddhism.explanation: The story shows a mourner discovering that sorrow is shared by the whole community.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife imagines the whole town sharing her sorrow; Kisa Gotami finds the whole town really does, and is freed by that knowledge.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 114 (Kisa Gotami) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very well-known story; good match on grief shared by a whole town, though the grief is for a child and the lesson is impermanence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “From desire of pleasure arises the misery of the whole world, the gods included; whatever misery of body and mind there is, the dispassionate will put an end to it.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana sees the misery of the whole world, not just one person, as springing from desire.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife imagines her sorrow spread over the whole town; Jain teaching agrees that such misery is universal, and traces it to desire.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches suffering as universal, but its point is diagnosis of desire, not shared grief at dusk.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Persephone is carried off, her mother Demeter grieves so deeply that she withholds growth from the earth, and the whole world suffers famine until her daughter is returned.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Homeric Hymn, one goddess’s grief at separation spreads until all of humanity shares in it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s wife feels her separation-grief spreading over the whole town; Demeter’s spreads over the whole earth.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter (Hymn 2) (paraphrase; cf. tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth; strong match on one person’s separation-grief afflicting everyone, though the bond is mother and daughter.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith argues that we come to feel others’ sorrows by imagining ourselves in their place, and that this sympathy is the root of shared moral feeling.
philosophy.explanation: Smith explains how one person’s grief can be reproduced, through imagination, in the hearts of others.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife runs the process in reverse: she imagines the whole town feeling what she feels at dusk.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I, section i, ch. 1 ‘Of Sympathy’ (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known argument; matches shared feeling through imagination, but Smith analyses sympathy rather than a lover’s projection.

kurals.tamil:
பொருள்மாலை யாளரை உள்ளி மருள்மாலை
மாயும்என் மாயா உயிர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Porulmaalai yaalarai ulli marulmaalai
maayumen maayaa uyir.
kurals.meaning: My life, which has survived until now, is dying in this bewildering evening as I think of him whose heart is set on gaining wealth.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a parent who works far away to earn money for the family. Even if it is for a good reason, the child at home can feel very lonely at night. The wife feels this way: her husband went to earn wealth, and in the evening she misses him so much it feels unbearable.
kurals.university: The closing couplet names the cause of the separation: the husband is poruḷ-mālaiyāḷar, ‘one whose nature (mālai) is wealth’, who has gone away to earn; Solomon Pappaiah sharpens this to ‘one for whom the delusion of wealth is everything’. The poet plays on mālai three ways, ‘nature, disposition’ in poruḷmālai, ‘evening’ in maruḷ mālai (‘bewildering dusk’), and by sound with māyum (‘dies’) and māyā (‘undying’): the life that did not perish (māyā uyir) through the separation so far now perishes (māyum) at this dusk. Varadarasanar glosses māyā uyir as a life that ‘stood as if by magic’ despite grief. Pope: ‘This darkening eve, my darkling soul must perish utterly; / Remembering him who seeks for wealth, but seeks not me.’ Both web sources give identical text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Offered wealth, long life and every pleasure by Yama, the boy Nachiketas refuses them all, saying that no man can be made happy by wealth and that he wants only the knowledge of what lies beyond death.
hinduism.explanation: The Katha Upanishad sets the pursuit of wealth below the pursuit of what truly matters.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s wife suffers because her husband has chosen wealth over her presence, the very trade-off Nachiketas refuses.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; matches wealth as a lesser good, but its higher good is spiritual knowledge, not married love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that the pursuit of wealth leads people astray and brings many sorrows.
christianity.tie_back: In the Kural, it is the wife who is ‘pierced with sorrows’ because her husband has gone after wealth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; matches wealth-seeking as a source of sorrow, though Paul speaks of the seeker’s own sorrows and the Kural does not condemn the husband.

islam.quote_or_event: “Competition in [worldly] increase diverts you Until you visit the graveyards.”
islam.explanation: Surat at-Takathur warns that the race for more distracts people from what matters until death overtakes them.
islam.tie_back: The wife sees her husband diverted by the pursuit of wealth while her own life ebbs away in the evening.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; matches wealth as a distraction from what matters, though the Qur’an’s concern is the hereafter.

judaism.explanation: Hillel, in Pirkei Avot, observes that increasing possessions brings increasing worry.
judaism.tie_back: In the Kural the anxiety falls on the wife left at home while her husband pursues property abroad.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:7 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (quoted in part); matches wealth bringing worry, but Hillel means the owner’s own anxiety.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That is not a strong fetter, the wise say, which is made of iron, wood or hemp. But the infatuation and longing for jewels and ornaments, children and wives — that, they say, is a far stronger fetter”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names longing for both wealth and family as the strongest of bonds.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s couple are held by both fetters at once: he by wealth, she by love for him, and the strain kills her at evening.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org (quoted in part); matches wealth and spouse as binding attachments, but recommends renouncing both.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Misery ceases on the absence of delusion, delusion ceases on the absence of desire, desire ceases on the absence of greed, greed ceases on the absence of property.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana traces misery back through a chain of causes that ends in property.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s whole chapter of misery begins with a husband who has gone after property, the first link in the Jain chain.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches property as the root of misery, though the Jain verse is a general doctrine, not a wife’s complaint.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus tells Penelope that her husband is alive and could have been home long ago, but chose to travel from land to land gathering wealth before returning.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer has the faithful wife hear that her husband’s long absence was stretched out by the pursuit of riches.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Penelope, the Kural’s wife waits, night after night, for a husband whose return is delayed by wealth-seeking.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 19.282-286 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; close match on a wife waiting while her husband gathers wealth abroad, though the tale is part of Odysseus’s disguise.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The life of money-making is one undertaken under compulsion, and wealth is evidently not the good we are seeking; for it is merely useful and for the sake of something else.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle ranks wealth as a mere means, never the final good of a human life.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s wife suffers because her husband is ‘a man of wealth’ by nature; Aristotle reminds us that wealth is only ever for the sake of something else, such as the shared life she is losing.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; matches wealth as a mere means, though Aristotle says nothing about love or separation.
